secondaryFeatures.title: s21e28: Did you try the app?
secondaryFeatures.author: Unknown
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
0.0 Context setting

Friday, September 4 2026 in Portland, Oregon where I have realised that I have finally become a certain kind of person. I’m sitting in a cafe prepping this morning’s How People Work, Live! for upload, which means I’ve got one tab with Descript open, another with Libsyn open, and thoughts about how much of this is web apps these days. There’s actually something nice about how Descript works -- the fact that it can import video straight from Zoom without having to go through the rigmarole of logging into Zoom, downloading several gigabytes worth of video and then uploading it back to Descript. Technically Descript is also able to upload the edited video back out to YouTube but, well, I don’t trust it because I’ve got a bunch of complicated stuff going on. Or at least I think I’ve got complicated stuff going on. The thing is, being able to import data from one service to another service without having to roundtrip it through the pipe that goes to my laptop is how things should work, but of course, it’s a surprise when things work that well.

All of which is a long way of saying that I am doing this in a cafe surrounded by what I feel, as a 46-year old, are Young People who are doing Shiny Young Things on their own laptops and iPads but I am suddenly here now also as a Content Creator. I am expending energy trying to deny this fact and feeling uncomfortable about it, and yet here we are.

(It is clearly not Friday. It’s Wednesday 9 September now.)

0.1 How People Work, Live!

I had a great time with Sarah Vieira this morning in today’s episode, it’s up on the podcast and YouTube now; you can catch up on anywhere RSS works with your podcast app, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

(124 subscribers on YouTube now! My kids will be super impressed. I will celebrate when I hit 200!)

Next up!

Friday 11 September at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Dana Chisnell

Dana Chisnell, a pioneering civic designer dedicated to improving government services through human-centered design. She was the first head of customer experience at the Department of Homeland Security. Dana co-founded the Center for Civic Design, where she led initiatives like the Field Guides to Ensuring Voter Intent, and designed the prototype that is the basis of nearly every digital ballot in the U.S. As a founding member of the U.S. Digital Service, Dana contributed to modernizing federal digital services. She has taught design in government at Harvard Kennedy School and co-authored the seminal Handbook of Usability Testing.

Friday 18 September at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Anna Pickard

Anna Pickard, a writer who does more talking about writing than writing. She mainly works as a consultant in Voice and Tone, helping companies sound human, and helping writing teams get their work done. After training in theatre, she worked in journalism, advertising and games, before stumbling into tech. From 2014, she was responsible for moulding, evolving and shaping the voice of Slack, and since leaving in 2020, has worked with Apple, Airbnb, Atlassian and a bunch of other companies that don’t begin with A.

Meanwhile, there’s the open How People Work... Does Happy Hour open clinic on Tuesdays at 1pm PT, where you get to bring what you’ve been thinking about and we chat about it as a small group.

1.0 Some Things That Caught My Attention

1.1 Did you try the app?

Here’s something that caught my attention: in the U.S., Walmart is rolling out its own electrical vehicle charging network. Just like elsewhere, turns out that one of the most valuable things you can own (or have possession/a license to) is property or real estate.

EVs are a particularly interesting case because if there’s a real transition to them, which there appears to be in the rest of the world, then charging coverage is helpful! It’s even more interesting when you realize that Walmart could also blanket their property in solar and then the cost of providing charging drops to (handwaves) something negligible.

Of course, it’s not that easy. Charging an EV is complicated, but one of the reasons why it’s complicated is to make it save. Amongst other things, there’s a whole network connection between the EV and charging station to make sure the right voltage and amps are being supplied, never mind a bunch of handshaking to ensure that the charging port is locked/unlocked. Then you can add payment on to that, too.

Oh, right. Payment. Because there’s a load of computers involved and we can’t help ourselves, that means that if you want to use Walmart’s EV charging network, you have to use... you guessed it: Walmart’s app! Which is why it is hilarious (derogatory) and unsurprising (exhaustedly) that you get coverage like this:

My First Walmart EV Charging Experience Was A Disaster: The company's public fast-charging station left me baking in the sun for 40 minutes1

I knew most Walmart stations didn’t have credit card readers yet, so I planned ahead. Before leaving, I downloaded the Walmart app, created an account, and added my credit card information so I could activate the charging session as soon as I arrived at the station. But activating a Walmart charger through its app was nothing like the experience at Tesla or, frankly, most other major charging networks.

Here’s a summary, at least from the article, about what went wrong:

  • The app’s QR code scanner failed to detect the code displayed on the charger to activate the charger
  • It wasn’t clear that you could select a charger without scanning a QR code
  • “the app was glitchy”
  • Instead of starting a charging session, they got a “something went wrong” error message
  • The metal buttons on the charger itself “felt like touching a hot skillet from sitting under the summer sun all day”
  • The app also threw another after scanning the QR code: “We’re having technical issues, try again in a moment”
  • The author tried initiating charging with the vehicle off (didn’t work) and then with it on again (because they know about issues with handshaking)
  • Calling customer service said the errors were “possibly due to connectivity problems” or “a Walmart app glitch”
  • Cellular connectivity wasn’t particularly strong at the site, but the customer’s other apps were working just fine
  • The customer was recommended to uninstall the app, reinstall the app, log back into the account (the same errors happened)... (the app is 451.7 MB on iOS)
  • and happened on an adjacent charger...

The user just gave up after 40 minutes and then went ton an Ionna Rechargery, where they did this:

“I simply tapped my phone on the card reader, plugged in the cable, and the bZ Woodland started charging in less than a minute after I pulled up to the charger.”

They also noticed that there was nobody using the Walmart chargers, but that “the Ionna station, meanwhile, was bustling”.

I love this article because the writer has totally done their homework and noticed that “both stations use the exact same charging hardware: Alpitronic HYC400s”.

“At Ionna, I could simply tap my card on the reader and start charging.”

Anyway, Walmart says they’re going to add “swipe and dip-to-ship terminals “at most locations”2, which makes everything OK.

This is the same Walmart that famously didn’t implement tap-to-pay at least, hasn’t implemented tap-to-pay until August this year3, preferring to push people towards using the Walmart App for tap-to-pay.

I mean, I’ll just say what I think is the obvious thing here: the digital strategy of having an app and, I don’t know a single touchpoint [sic] to provide a unified customer experience [sic] is fine until it becomes a load-bearing liability [sic] 4.

The whole point of a charging network and an EV charger is of course to charge a car. There’s a car charger at the Oregon Aquarium out on the coast that I occasionally use and it too needs an app for you to use it, only the thing is the app also requires network connectivity. And the network connectivity out in the carpark is shiiiiiit. So it always takes ages to get a connection and start charging. This is not ideal! It’s really kind of annoying!

It’s incredibly frustrating to imagine the kind of meetings and management and leadership decisions at Walmart that led up to this state of affairs. I get that someone somewhere has said it’s super great to own the relationship [sic] with a customer and get them to spend a bunch of time in the Walmart app. Sure, great. I get it. But, like, it’s got to be good? You only have a certain level of goodwill, and clearly there’s a choice of EV chargers what with in this instance a bunch of Ionna ones being nearby that actually work. It’s this attitude of a lack of agency: we don’t trust you to just pay with a card or tap to pay (which, to be clear! You could just associate the card with the account anyway! How do you think you keep getting receipts whenever you use a certain point of sale terminal!), no, you need to use our app. Which in this case is not better. It’s worse.

It’s also this drive for more and more and more data. Presumably someone out in Walmart corporate wants to know as much as possible about their customers. Forcing people to use their app to charge means, well, you have to use the app. Which means (let me just check the iOS details) it gets to track your location, your usage data, health and fitness, “sensitive info”, “identifiers” and so on.

Feels like a while ago people were either aware of this trade-off and didn’t care that much, but some sort of threshold has been tripped what with in the U.S. at least all these Flock cameras and decreasing autonomy and agency. You don’t get a choice anymore. You have to use the app, you can’t pay for it, and it’s like there’s a whole surveillance pressure. It is as if in some cases the whole “if you’re not paying, you’re the product” has seeped through into just general distrust. Plus the whole deal with all this digital transformation bullshit is that every company needs to actively expend energy to resist grabbing as much data about you as possible. It’s all just out there! Why not just track it! Why not just record it?

All you want to do is charge a car. All you want to do is watch TV without, you know, your TV using automated content recognition to report back what you’re watching. I mean, what the fuck? How is this OK? This is implicitly OK because, what, the TVs are cheap now and it’s in the terms of service? And then one of the responses to this is: well, you know, it’s not just LG TVs that are doing this, they all do this and they’ve been doing this for ages, so why are you freaking out about it now?

It is as if people have been marinating in some sort of internet miasma of personal information and as it’s been collected for, frankly, questionable benefit other than “free stuff”, the temperature has increased and increased until, I don’t know. People are snapping and driving around destroying surveillance cameras. (Weirdly -- or not, they’re only destroying some kinds of cameras because those ones have had slightly more successful and pointed marketing than the other ones that do exactly the same thing).

This isn’t about the technology, though. It is about and has always been about power. The technology is the way to acquire power, to protect power, to consolidate power, to exercise power.

All that guy wanted to do was charge his car.

That’s it!

How are you doing? I mean, everything’s going great, right? Right?

Best,

Dan

  1. My First Walmart EV Charging Experience Was A Disaster (archive.is), Suvat Kothari, Inside EVs, 3 September 2026 ↩

  2. Walmart’s Expanding EV Charging Network Is Getting Easier To Pay For (And Cheaper) (archive.is), Iulian Dnistran, Inside EVs, 26 May 2026 ↩

  3. Here's when tap to pay is coming to Walmart, Sam's Club (archive.is), Gabe Hauari, USA Today, 27 August 2026 ↩

  4. Did you see what I did there. I used the phrase “load-bearing” knowing that it’s a thing the LLMs. Ha ha ha. ↩

secondaryFeatures.title: Donald Trump Lies a Lot About 9/11
secondaryFeatures.author: Parker Molloy
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
On Tuesday, at an event honoring 9/11 first responders, President Donald Trump told a story about being picked up off the ground and carried away by two firemen after the terrorist attack 25 years ago.

“For nine months, rescue and recovery crews worked day and night on the site. I want to just thank my people; I took a lot of my me(n) — I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened. And they were — they had no hesitation — everybody went down with me. We went down, it was a big group of people. Wasn’t too much we could do, I’ll be honest — it was, you know, it was raw, and nobody’s seen anything like it, ever.

We had other buildings; the United States Steel building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down; the truth is it creaked a lot, it creaked. It still creaks. But it never came down, and I re(member) — I’ll never forget two firemen. We thought it was coming down on top of us, and two firemen — big, strong guys — and I’m not the smallest guy in the world — they grabbed me under the arms, said, ‘Gotta get out of here.’ And they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do. I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself.’ But they were amazing, but they thought it was coming down; it didn’t come down. US Steel.”

One Liberty Plaza — formerly known as the U.S. Steel Building — is located at 165 Broadway, across from the site of where the Twin Towers once stood. It reopened about a month and a half after the attack, after its owner Brookfield Properties announced that a preliminary review by independent structural engineers had found no damage to the building’s structure. Aside from some damage to the building’s facade (they replaced hundreds of windows on the west side of the building), it was completely fine. Trump’s claim that “it still creaks” is odd, as people have been going to work in the building every weekday for the past 25 years without incident.

CNN’s Daniel Dale fact checked Trump’s claim, finding there to be “no basis“ for it. No, Trump wasn’t close to the World Trade Center on the day of the attack. No, there’s no evidence that Trump was in the U.S. Steel Building in the immediate aftermath of 9/11, either. While there was some initial worry that the U.S. Steel Building might have structural damage in the days after the attacks, there’s no evidence that Trump was there.

He’s been building on this story for a quarter century

On September 13, 2001, in an interview with NBC, Trump shared the first iteration of the tale:

“Well, not only is it devastation, but it’s very dangerous. Because every few minutes, a whistle will go off and everybody would just run, because you have all the buildings around it, which are in such a weakened state, that people just don’t know.

And so, they just have to take off, and then they come back, and they’re working under 50-story buildings that you don’t know if... if they’re going to fall down. So, it’s a terrible thing for the workers and it’s a terrible thing for the world, really.”

In the interview, Trump says that he has “hundreds of men inside working right now, and we’re bringing down another 125 in a little while.” Asked how his men were holding up, he talked about the rescue effort finding survivors — “like the five firemen that they just found a little while ago” — without ever saying his own crew was the one doing the finding. While Trump has bragged about having men at the scene, there is no evidence that this actually happened.

But what’s interesting about this quote isn’t the lie about him having a crew down there, but the fact that he described the chaos in buildings near ground zero as happening to other people, not him. “Everybody would just run, because you have all the buildings around it, which are in such a weakened state that people just don’t know.” Everybody runs, but he’s not one of them. Later in the same interview, describing the men digging through the rubble: “And above them you have 55-story buildings that are very possibly going to be pouring down on them any minute.” On them.

Then, fourteen years later during a campaign stop in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, Trump shared a slightly different version of the story. Now he was a part of it.

“And I was there when we actually thought the U.S. Steel Building was coming down and I’ll never forget that I was standing next to these two massive wonderful firemen and we heard a screech, like a screech, steel on steel and it was a couple of days after the buildings and I was down there with the — we had a crew of people that, you know, to help.

I mean it’s — they needed a lot of help. I’ve never seen anything like I saw, and they heard a screech, and everybody thought that the U.S. Steel Building was coming down and it was not so far from us. And these two guys there were massive guys, two really big — because I’m a big guy and they grabbed me. I must tell you honestly, I never knew I could run that fast. I — but they were running just as fast and they had my arms and they were and we were just running.”

It’s evolved. He’s now at the scene with his crew, and here’s the first appearance of the two firemen. But look at what he says they actually did. They grabbed his arms, and he ran — so fast that he surprised himself. He also gives you a date, “a couple of days after the buildings,” and a location: “not so far from us.” He’s outside the building.

Five years after that, on Newsmax, the story changes again.

“I was down there right after the event, and I brought a big crew of people down. And I helped. A lot of other people helped. Those first responders are very brave. And I’m telling you, we were hearing creaks — I’ve never forgotten it. There was, I think, the United States Steel Building, it was called at the time, and it’s 50 stories tall. And we heard creaks. I said, ‘that building is going to come down,’ and two big firemen grabbed me, grabbed other people. It never came down, but I never heard a noise like that. It was a scary situation.”

Okay. Sure. But then, by Tuesday, the qualifiers were gone. No date. No “not so far from us.” Nobody else getting grabbed. And Trump wasn’t running anymore — he was being carried.

Share

He can’t stop lying about 9/11

Hours after the towers fell on 9/11, Trump called in to WWOR-TV. Someone asked him about the condition of one of his buildings, 40 Wall Street. He said this:

“40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually, before the World Trade Center, was the tallest — and then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.”

Now, this might seem like a really callous thing to brag about on 9/11, but what makes it even more bizarre is the fact that 40 Wall Street was not actually the tallest building in lower Manhattan. 70 Pine was still 25 feet taller than 40 Wall Street. And while that seems like a trivial thing to take issue with, I think it’s indicative of Trump’s tendency to make things up.

In November 2015, Trump said during a campaign rally in Columbus, Ohio, that he personally witnessed people jump out of the towers on 9/11, watching from his apartment:

“Many people jumped and I witnessed it, I watched that. I have a view — a view in my apartment that was specifically aimed at the World Trade Center. And I watched those people jump and I watched the second plane hit ... I saw the second plane hit the building and I said, ‘Wow that’s unbelievable.’”

Two days earlier, at a rally in Birmingham, Alabama, Trump told the audience that he “watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down. And I watched in Jersey City, New Jersey, where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down. Thousands of people were cheering.” He doubled down on the line during an interview with ABC News’ This Week. There is no evidence that there were “thousands and thousands of people” cheering the 9/11 attacks.

In Buffalo in April 2016, Trump publicly claimed that he was personally at ground zero clearing rubble (this is the same speech where he accidentally referred to it as 7-Eleven instead of 9/11):

“These people were going through terror and you know what happened. Everyone who helped clear the rubble. And I was there and I watched and I helped a little bit. But I want to tell you, those people were amazing. Clearing the rubble, trying to find additional lives. You didn’t know what was gonna come down on all of us and they handled it. Every small act of kindness, every great act of courage, those are New York values, OK? So when a guy like lying Ted Cruz talks about, talks about New York values folks, those are the values that we want to talk about.”

On July 29, 2019, during an event permanently authorizing the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund, speaking to a crowd of first responders, Trump made sure to say that while he doesn’t consider himself a first responder, he was totally there.

“In a few moments, I will sign the 9/11 Victims Compensation Fund. This law makes permanent the financial support for families who lost precious loved ones as a result of September 11th attacks. It also provides pensions for those who are suffering from cancer and other illnesses stemming from the toxic debris they were exposed to in the aftermath of the attacks. Many of those affected were firefighters, police officers, and other first responders. And I was down there also, but I’m not considering myself a first responder. But I was down there. I spent a lot of time down there with you.”

The next day, Richard Alles, who was an FDNY battalion chief on September 11 and spent months on the site in its aftermath, spoke with PolitiFact, telling them, “I was there for several months — I have no knowledge of his being down there.” And if Trump had sent a crew of 100 workers, “there would be a record of it. Everybody worked under direct supervision of the police and fire department and the joint commander for emergency services. Is there a chance he was ever down there by himself and I didn’t know it? It’s possible, but I know of no one who ever witnessed him there.” Alles, who is now director of 9/11 community affairs at the law firm Barasch and McGarry, which represents people filing Victim Compensation Fund claims, also told PolitiFact that Trump’s line about being at ground zero was not on the Teleprompter.

While speaking at the Pentagon on the 18th anniversary of 9/11, Trump said:

“I was sitting at home watching a major business television show early that morning. Jack Welch, the legendary head of General Electric, was about to be interviewed when all of the sudden they cut away. At first there were different reports. ‘It was a boiler fire.’ But I knew that boilers aren’t at the top of a building. ‘It was a kitchen explosion in Windows of the World.’ Nobody really knew what happened. There was great confusion.

I was looking out from a building in midtown Manhattan directly at the World Trade Center when I saw a second plane, at a tremendous speed, go into the second tower.

Soon after, I went down to ground zero with men who worked for me to try to help in any little way that we could. We were not alone. So many others were scattered around trying to do the same, they were all trying to help.”

Trump Tower is more than 4 miles away from ground zero. He almost certainly could not see people jumping from the towers with the naked eye. It’s possible he’s confusing this with TV coverage he watched.

And then just this past Sunday, Trump appeared on Fox News:

“I had an apartment where I’m viewing the World Trade Center from midtown. I was downtown, but it’s not very far when the building is 115 stories tall. And I’m viewing this thing happen, and I’m saying, ‘That’s crazy. Couldn’t be a plane. Maybe it was a missile.’

And then I saw the second plane hit, and you saw that coming, and you’re watching it and it’s — because I watched the air patterns for years, and you know where the planes are, they go right up the Hudson River. This thing was coming right into the second building. And I said, ‘Wow!’ So I watched that happen, and I said ‘Wow, we are now in a different time.’ So I saw it and I said ‘The world has just changed.’ And I went down. I was building a building in New York and I had a lot of construction workers, and I went shortly after, the following day. You couldn’t go down the same day. But, like the following day. Very quickly afterwards, and we worked long and hard.”

That’s a lot of bullshit from just one guy.
